liturgical_day: Thursday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: A net gathering fish of every kind
theme: Christ's net gathers widely in the present age, but the final shore reveals what each life has become; disciples who understand this judgment must draw faithfully from the whole treasure of revelation.
introduction: Jesus closes his kingdom parables beside the sea with an image of sweeping breadth and sober consequence. A net receives fish of every kind before anyone sorts the catch. For now, the kingdom's proclamation reaches through the mixed waters of the world, gathering people without pretending that every life is already whole. At the shore comes the separation that only God can finally accomplish. Yet Jesus does not leave his disciples merely afraid: he asks whether they understand, then entrusts them with a householder's work. They are to bring forth treasures both new and old, reading all that God has given in the light of the kingdom now revealed in Christ.
hero_alt: First-century fishermen drawing a vast net of many kinds of fish toward a luminous shore as Christ teaches his disciples nearby, rendered in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and restrained luminous geometry
closing_title: Live now in light of the shore
closing: The net is already moving through the sea, and none of us sees the whole catch as God sees it. Christ therefore forbids both complacency and premature judgment. It is not enough merely to have been gathered within hearing of the Gospel; faith must take flesh in a life turned toward the good. Nor are disciples appointed to perform the angels' final separation before its time. Their present task is to receive the kingdom deeply, teach it faithfully, and bring from the one divine treasury what is new and what is old. The last judgment gives urgency to conversion, while the householder's abundance gives courage: God has supplied his Church with truth sufficient for the journey to the shore.

verses.text: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering together every kind of fish.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: The Church's net reaches into the troubled waters of the world and calls every condition of person toward forgiveness. Its breadth is real, even while the final quality of the catch remains to be revealed.
verses.commentary: Gregory understands the sea as the unstable present world and the net as the Holy Church entrusted to fishers. Through her proclamation, people are drawn away from the depths of eternal death and called toward the heavenly kingdom. The catch includes every kind: wise and foolish, free and enslaved, rich and poor, strong and weak. The verse therefore displays the generous reach of the call without claiming that all who enter the net are already alike in holiness. Until history is complete, the Church gathers a mixed people, carrying them together toward the place where every life will be brought fully into the light.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 11 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: When it was filled, they drew it out; and sitting by the shore, they chose the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: The shore signifies history's end, when the mixed condition of the present Church gives way to manifest judgment. What the net has carried together will not remain forever undistinguished.
verses.commentary: Gregory reads the net's fullness as the completion of the human race and the shore as the end of the world. During the voyage, faith's net contains good and bad together, so outward membership alone does not disclose the final truth of a life. Once the catch reaches land, however, the good are received into the vessels of eternal dwelling, while those who have rejected the kingdom's inward light are cast away. The image warns against confusing present mixture with final indifference. It also places the separation at the shore: the Church gathers now, while definitive judgment belongs to the end toward which God draws history.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 11 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: So shall it be at the end of the world. The angels shall go out and separate the wicked from among the just.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Jesus interprets his own parable: the sorting is the angels' work at the end of the world. The warning concerns not merely hearing the Gospel, but allowing faith to shape one's life.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom distinguishes this net from the earlier parables. Some lose the seed through inattention, and the weeds signify corrupt teaching; here the danger is an evil life maintained even after a person has been gathered through knowledge of God. Christ therefore prevents his hearers from treating mere contact with preaching as sufficient. At the end, the angels separate the wicked from among the just, carrying out the judgment God appoints. The verse gives moral seriousness to belonging: divine truth is meant to be lived. Yet it also reserves final separation for God's servants at the appointed time, not for human impatience within the present age.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, Homily 47 on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: And they shall cast them into the furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: The parable's final warning is deliberately plain. Christ names judgment openly so that no hearer can mistake the eternal seriousness of conversion.
verses.commentary: Gregory counsels fear here more than speculative explanation, because Christ states the punishment of sinners without disguise. The furnace, weeping, and gnashing of teeth make the warning unmistakable; no one can excuse indifference by claiming that the consequence was hidden beneath an obscure image. Such fear is not an invitation to despair, but a summons to take grace and repentance seriously while there is time. The same Lord who casts the net widely also tells the truth about refusing the good for which we were gathered. His severity awakens the conscience, so that the hearer may turn toward mercy rather than discover judgment only at the shore.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 11 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: Have you understood all these things? They said to him: “Yes.”
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Jesus asks the disciples for understanding because they will soon teach others. A disciple must receive the mystery inwardly, not merely hear the same words as the crowd.
verses.commentary: Jerome emphasizes that the question is addressed especially to the Apostles. Christ does not intend them to remain at the level of listeners in the crowd; because they will teach, they must grasp what the parables disclose. Their “Yes” marks both a gift received and a responsibility accepted. Understanding the kingdom is not private mastery or cleverness, but preparation for faithful service. The Lord first explains judgment, then examines his future teachers before describing their treasury. Anyone who hands on the Gospel must therefore listen beneath its familiar surface, allow Christ's words to judge the heart, and speak from understanding formed in the presence of the Teacher.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: He said to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”
verses.author: St Hilary of Poitiers
verses.insight: The instructed disciple draws from one treasury in which Law and Gospel belong together. What is old and what is new have the same divine owner and find their unity in Christ.
verses.commentary: Hilary says Christ calls the disciples scribes because they have understood the teaching set before them. Their treasure contains new and old: the Gospel and the Law, not as rival possessions but as gifts belonging to the same householder. Christ even compares these instructed servants to himself, for their capacity to teach comes from the treasury of his Holy Spirit. The disciple's task is therefore neither to discard what God formerly revealed nor to repeat it without the light of fulfillment. Faithful teaching brings both forth in their proper unity, showing how the kingdom newly manifested in Christ completes rather than contradicts God's long preparation of his people.
verses.source_label: St Hilary of Poitiers, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: And it came to pass that, when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: After revealing the parables to the people and their meaning to the disciples, Jesus moves on to teach elsewhere. Understanding is meant to accompany him into mission.
verses.commentary: Jerome notes the movement that follows the discourse: after speaking the parables publicly and granting understanding to the Apostles, Jesus departs for his own country to teach there as well. The verse is more than a narrative pause. Revelation does not remain fixed beside one shoreline, and discipleship cannot turn a moment of insight into a place of rest. Christ carries the word onward, including toward those who may receive him poorly. His teachers, newly described as householders with a rich treasury, must follow that same pattern. What they understand in private is given for the patient work of proclamation wherever the Lord goes next.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea
